name: Targeted Review: Productive Failure & Thematic Issues Titles
description: Saved literature review featuring cleaned and restored titles for Productive Failure and Thematic Issues interdisciplinary course design papers.

papers.title: Learning in Productive Failure
papers.abstract: In Productive Failure (PF), students are prepared for subsequent  instruction by activating prior knowledge and becoming aware of own knowledge gaps when generating solution attempts to an unknown problem. Intermediate knowledge after solution generation likely affords the subsequent integration of new knowledge, but has only seldom been assessed in composite instructional designs such as PF. We investigated how the learning processes and (intermediate) knowledge in PF vary when manipulating the PF tasks’ goal formulations (learning vs. problem -solving goals). As hypothesized, learning goals led to higher gap awareness prior to instruction, higher closing of gaps after instruction as well as better learning outcomes compared to the problem -solving goals. Moreover, broad knowledge activation during the first learning phase correlated with the intermediate knowledge state. Contrary to our hypotheses, knowledge activation and gap awareness did not mediate the learning outcomes.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Learning in Productive Failure: How Knowledge Gap Awareness and Intermediate Knowledge Link Prior Knowledge Activation and Conceptual Knowledge. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and sentiments in interdisciplinary and productive failure designs.

papers.title: Thematic Issues: Three Design Models to Address The Challenge of
papers.authors: Selma Hamdani, Elizabeth S. Charles, Annie-Helene Samson
papers.abstract: The increasing complexity of societal challenges requires interdisciplinary approaches in education to cultivate critical thinking, adaptability, and a holistic understanding of global issues. In response, the  Quebec college system’s Social Science program introduced the Thematic Issues course (TI), a single -instructor course designed to engage students in interdisciplinary inquiry through instructor- selected themes and three prescribed social science disciplines. To navigate the challenges of teaching across disciplines in an unstructured framework, instructors formed a Faculty Learning Community (FLC) to collaboratively refine course design and instructional strategies. This paper e xamines three TI course models: the serial model, offering compartmentalized insights; the spiral model, promoting cumulative, integrated learning; and the jigsaw model emphasizes collaborative synthesis by combining specialized disciplinary perspectives into a cohesive understanding. By analyzing these models, this practice-centered study highlights the pedagogical affordances and constraints of single-teacher interdisciplinary instruction. Context As societal issues grow more complex, interdisciplinary education is increasingly recognized as a way to help learners make sense of them. Curricula must prepare students for real -world challenges by fostering critical thinking, adaptability, and transferable skills (Peiqi & Xionghu, 2003). This paper presents a practitioner-centered perspective on the development of a multidiscipline course aimed at fostering interdisciplinary thinking. The course was collaboratively designed through the efforts of nine instructors (practitioners) at a large urban college in Quebec, part of the province’s unique 2-year post-secondary CEPEP system (1). These individuals were tasked with developing and teaching the first cohort of a 45-hour, third semester Social Science course called Thematic Issues (TI), which prepares students for a self- directed interdisciplinary project in their final ( fourth) semester. As a core course within the program, the TI is offered in 20 sections annually, serving approximately 500 students. Operating as a Faculty Learning Community ( FLC; to be defined shortly), the nine instructors brought expertise from six disciplines: psychology, anthropology, philosophy, religious studies, sociology, and business administration. These instructors had no experience working within an explicit theoretical framework to prepare for the design of the interdisciplinary course. Beginning in late May 2024, the instructors held initial meetings of the FLC before pausing for the summer, during which independent course planning took place. Bi-weekly meetings resumed in Fall 2024, leading to the course's first large scale offering that semester. This piloting phase is currently ongoing (Winter 2025) and will extend into Fall 2025. Early design decisions were driven by pragmatic reasoning and practitioner insights. However, one FLC member––the first author —was simultaneously involved in a research-practice partnership focused on interdisciplinary instruction, allowing for the integration of research-informed insights of this process. Inasmuch, her role is characterized as that of boundary spanner (Akkerman & Bakker, 2011), bridging theory to practice and enriching the FLC’s pedagogical approach to interdisciplinary course design. The faculty learning community Drawing on the Cox model of Faculty Learning Community (Cox, 2004), an FLC is a structured, collaborative group of educators who engage in an ongoing, scholarly, and collegial process to enhance teaching, learning and professional development (Richlin & Essington, 2004). This participatory approach offers several advantages including fostering interdisciplinary collaboration, enhancing teaching practices and building a supportive 2223 professional network that drives innovation in pedagogy. Participating in an FLC not only enhances individual teaching practices but also fosters a sense of community and professional growth among instructors (Cox, 2004). The FLC participants consisted of instructors who were either assigned to teach the TI course or who were involved in its initial design. Course development began with a shared understanding of the course competencies. Over the summer, each instructor independently designed their course based on their interpretation of the  course competency and learning o utcomes. In Fall 2024, during biweekly FLC meetings, instructors collaboratively refined their course designs, addressing challenges and aligning their approaches before implementing them in their classrooms. As noted earlier, the central challenge faced by this FLC stemmed from the nature of the TI course itself. With its open framework and minimal prescriptive guidance, the course placed the responsibility on individual instructors to independently design innovative pedagogical approaches that integrate diverse disciplinary perspectives. This task w as further complicated by the fact that, like many post -secondary educators, the instructors lacked formal training in teaching and learning (Ramolula, & Nkoane, 2024) —what is often referred to as the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL). Moreover, the course required them to engage with content and perspectives beyond their own disciplinary expertise. These were just some of the issues the nine FLC members grappled with during their many meetings, which ultimately shaped the course design described in the next section. Course design The initial results of the FLC were five proposals for the TI course design, these were subsequently refined to three models—Serial (Figure 1), Spiral (Figure 1), and Jigsaw (Figure 2)—each representing one of possible ways of addressing the interdisciplinary teaching challenge . These models were developed through instructors' experiential insights and collaborative brainstorming sessions . In large part, the FLC  instructors’ pragmatic practices and considerations of feasibility were the driving decision makers to settle on choosing these three designs as the models to be piloted . Once decided by the FLC, the first author brought them to the research - practice group for deeper study, leading to the identification of feature s that suggest alignment with known learning sciences theories and instructional strategies. Case 1: Serial model The serial model (Figure 1) follows a low-integration multidisciplinary structure, where students explore themes sequentially, with instructors acting as content experts (Jacobs, 1989).  In this model, each discipline is presented independently, allowing students to engage with multiple perspectives before drawing comparisons. This compartmentalized approach provides clarity but limits synthesis, positioning students as passive observers . While some instructors viewed this structure as a barrier to interdisc iplinary learning, others found it beneficial for students unfamiliar with interdisciplinary work, as it offers a structured introduction before deeper integration. Case 2: Spiral model The spiral model (Figure 1)  adopts a high- integration interdisciplinary approach, reinforcing cumulative understanding through iterative learning cycles, reminiscent  of Bruner’s (1960) spiral curriculum  approach. It engages students in recursive knowledge  construction, aligning with authentic complexity of real -world issues (e.g. mental health and wellbeing, climate change). This course design begins by establishing foundational knowledge of a central theme. It then progressively incorporates additional layers, examining how various factors —such as cultural contexts, developmental stages, and systemic influences —shape and inte ract with the core concept. These elements are explored as interconnected components that contribute to a broader understanding. Each stage builds upon the previous one, creating a cohesive framework that enables students to apply their earlier learning to increasingly complex ideas. 2224 Figure 1 The Serial and Spiral Models The serial model (left) presents disciplines sequentially, examining themes in isolation before drawing connections, while the spiral model (right) interweaves disciplines, revisiting core themes at increasing depths for a cumulative and integrated understanding. Case 3: Jigsaw model The jigsaw model (Figure 2), rooted in the cooperative learning framework (Aronson, et. al 1978; Johnson, et al., 2000), structures the TI course into two distinct phases. In the first phase, spanning the first 10 weeks of the semester, students are introduced to disciplinary concepts sequentially , much like in the serial mode. This phase establishes the foundational understanding of the course material. The final five weeks , the second phase, adopts a Jigsaw approach, where students are divided into groups  to explore a specific social science discipline’s perspective. This model engages students in collaborative synthesis, requiring them to actively contribute while instructors balance facilitation with content e xpertise. The Jigsaw model fosters student agency and interdependence, deepening critical thinking through peer teaching (Aronson et al., 1978). Figure 2 The Jigsaw Model This figure begins with a serial presentation of religion, introducing foundational concepts through three distinct components of the scientific study of religion. This is followed by an example showcasing the anthropology team's focused analysis, demonstrating their exploration of religious practices. The exemplar represents the discipline- specific deep dive, a critical step in the collaborative integration process that defines the jigsaw model. Conclusion 2225 Designed as a foundation for interdisciplinary learning, the TI course guides students in examining contemporary issues from multiple disciplinary perspectives, helping them develop the analytical skills needed for integrative thinking. The development of the TI course models emerged from ongoing collaboration between a practitioner FLC and a research-practice team, mediated by a facilitator who acted as a boundary spanner . Using an FLC approach, nine instructors collaborated to identify key challenges in interdisciplinary instruction and develop practical solutions for the TI course design. These discussions, informed by insights from the facilitator––working with the research team ––led to the identification of three pedagogical models —serial, spiral, and jigsaw —each offering a distinct approach to the challenge of interdisciplinary learning. Importantly, they demonstrate that the grounded and pragmatic solutions generated by practitioners can also be  justified by the learning sciences research. In doing so,  these models could act as boundary objects that allow both the FLC and the research - practice groups to examine the implications of the course designs on interdisciplinary learning. Results from the initial pilot of the TI course revealed that most instructors adhered to the serial model, likely due to its simple structure. However, two instructors from the FLC took the opportunity to experiment with the more interdisciplinary approaches – one implementing the spiral model and the other the jigsaw model. The instructor who opted for the spiral model highlighted its effectiveness in fostering knowledge integration . In reflecting on the experience of working within this model the instructor stated that it allowed her to reflect more "authentic real -world situations" into her class activities (Participant 2, personal communication, [2025]) . By examining core themes from different disciplinary perspectives, it helps students integrate the knowledge in meaningful ways that resemble solving authentic problems. The Spiral model was praised for its effectiveness in fostering deep understanding and sustained engagement. The instructor also noted that it required significant time to plan the curricular activities . The other instructor, who adopted the jigsaw model, reported high student engagement. However, during an FLC discussion, concerns were raised about the challenge of managing the integration of the six disciplines within the exercise (recall Fig 2) disciplines within this model. Despite the challenges, he was encouraged by the results of the jigsaw model and proposed exploring modifications to improve its feasibility, including a more purposeful selection of disciplines to enhance the coherence of the activity. From the perspective of the practitioner, these three TI course models offer flexible feasible frameworks that can be adapted to various institutional and disciplinary contexts and offer valuable insights for educators seeking to foster integrative learning across disciplines. The Serial Model, with its discipline-specific sequencing, may be most suitable for institutions where interdisciplinary coordination is limited but can serve as a first step toward integration. The Spiral Model, which builds on iterative engagement with interdisciplinary themes, requires sustained collaboration but offers a scalable approach for programs aiming to deepen integration over time. The Jigsaw Model, emphasizing cooperative learning, is highly adaptable to settings that prioritize student- centered learning and active engagement. From the perspective of learning sciences, these models are opportunities for research to examine how they function across different educational contexts and their impact on student learning outcomes, allowing us  to better understand their effectiveness in fostering interdisciplinary thinking. Additionally, further investigation could explore the extent to which the models align with constructivist and social constructivist principles, identifying potential affordances within their designs that may enhance interdisciplinary learning. From a facilitation perspective, the FLC approach proved to be a valuable mechanism for supporting interdisciplinary course design. It enabled the development, refinement, and implementation of the three course design models while fostering a collaborative space for pedagogical innovation. The role of the facilitator was particularly crucial in maintaining a focus on interdisciplinary learning objectives. A key challenge involved balancing instructional design priorities with the traditionally content- driven orientation of higher education instructors. As this project continues, ongoing analysis in collaboration with the research- practice group will further examine the effectiveness of these models and refine their implementation, particularly within the context of an FLC. Endnotes (1)  The CEGEP (Collège d'Enseignement Général et Professionnel) is unique to Quebec, Canada. It serves as a bridge between secondary education and higher education. It offers two- year pre-university programs or three-year technical programs. CEGEPs emphasize accessibility and affordability. They offer ablend of specialized as well as general education. papers.title: Sowing Seeds for Applying Productive Failure to Reading: Pre-Reading Questions Alone are Not Enough to Reap the Benefits
papers.authors: Zack Carpenter, Jennifer Cromley, Martin Van Boekel
papers.abstract: There is no know n work mapping Productive Failure  (PF)—a popular pedagogical design within the Learning Sciences—to reading. Therefore, through a secondary data analysis of students reading several expository biology excerpts, the current work attempts to bridge PF and reading. One group of students answered questions before reading the passages, while the other group did not. The results revealed that pre -reading questions had no effect on the acquisition of causal language, but the different passages did affect causal language pickup. Productive failure and prereading questions Evidence suggests that embracing failure in educational settings promotes learning (Williams-Pierce et al., 2021), with Productive Failure (PF) being one effective learning design (Sinha & Kapur, 2021). PF studies demonstrate enhanced learning, particularly in STEM (Sinha & Kapur, 2021), but there's limited exploration in non -STEM areas despite calls for such research (Loibl et al., 2017). Our focus  here is on applying PF to reading through examining the impact of prereading questions on understanding causa l language pickup (Cromley et al., 2020). While there's no direct link between PF and reading, we argue prereading questions are one bridge  (Lewis & Mensink, 2012). Bringing together PF and reading offers a generative opportunity for the Learning Sciences, especially because there are apparent shared mechanisms. Productive Failure involves two phases: (1) a problem- solving phase where students generate solutions to a complex problem they don't know how to solve, leading to initial failure, and (2) a direct instruction phase introducing the canonical  solution (Sinha & Kapur, 2021). It incorporates design considerations across the activity, participation structures, and social surround. Students in PF activities often outperform those receiving instruction first, and the mechanisms said to contribute to PF's effectiveness include activating prior knowledge, highlighting critical conceptual features, explaining and elaborating on concepts, and organizing critical features into concepts (Sinha & Kapur, 2021). Pre-reading questions influence reading processes, including the identification of causal language crucial for forming a comprehensive situation model (Cromley et al., 2020). The situation model is a mental construct of the text that extends beyond the comprehension of individual words and sentences. Considering some mechanisms in the context of Productive Failure (PF), this research  investigates how prereading questions influence the identification of causal language.  Firstly, answering questions before reading a text can activate pertinent prior knowledge about a topic (Alemi & Ebadi, 2010). We predict that this activation will prompt readers to notice relevant causal language necessary to answer the questions while they are reading the text. Secondly, we anticipate that readers will be drawn to pre-reading related text elements , thereby increasing the likelihood of identifying the causal language within the text (Lewis & Mensink, 2012) . With these two mechanistic predictions in mind, we pose the following research question: Do prereading questions lead to greater identification of causal language during the reading process?
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Sowing Seeds for Applying Productive Failure to Reading: Pre-Reading Questions Alone are Not Enough to Reap the Benefits. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and sentiments in interdisciplinary and productive failure designs.

papers.title: Trajectories of Feelings Toward Failure: Undergraduate Data Visualization Students’ Longitudinal Sentiments Towards a Productive Failure Design
papers.abstract: Productive Failure (PF) is a learning design where students tackle challenging, open- ended problems before receiving instruction, often leading to initial "failure" (i.e., an inability to discover the canonical solution completely). Afterward, they are taught the targeted concepts. Research shows that this approach, when following certain principles, promotes deeper learning compared to instruction-first methods. However, the long-term effects of PF and students' feelings of it remain underexplored. This study examines the longitudinal impact of PF in an undergraduate data visualization course, focusing on student experiences and comparing PF-based instruction to traditional teaching methods.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Trajectories of Feelings Toward Failure: Undergraduate Data Visualization Students’ Longitudinal Sentiments Towards a Productive Failure Design. **Finding**: Empirical study investigating learning and sentiments in interdisciplinary and productive failure designs.
